# Self-Steering Deep Non-Linear Spatially Selective Filters for Efficient Extraction of Moving Speakers under Weak Guidance Thanks: This work was supported by the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG, German Research Foundation) under grant 508337379 and Erlangen National High Performance Computing Center (NHR@FAU) of the Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU) under the NHR project f104ac. NHR funding is provided by federal and Bavarian state authorities. NHR@FAU hardware is partially funded by the DFG under grant 440719683.

###### Abstract

Recent works on deep non-linear spatially selective filters demonstrate
exceptional enhancement performance with computationally lightweight
architectures for stationary speakers of known directions. However, to
maintain this performance in dynamic scenarios, resource-intensive
data-driven tracking algorithms become necessary to provide precise
spatial guidance conditioned on the initial direction of a target
speaker. As this additional computational overhead hinders application
in resource-constrained scenarios such as real-time speech enhancement,
we present a novel strategy utilizing a low-complexity tracking
algorithm in the form of a [pf](#id41) instead. Assuming a causal,
sequential processing style, we introduce temporal feedback to leverage
the enhanced speech signal of the [ssf](#id31) to compensate for the
limited modeling capabilities of the [pf](#id41). Evaluation on a
synthetic dataset illustrates how the [ar](#id34) interplay between both
algorithms drastically improves tracking accuracy and leads to strong
enhancement performance. A listening test with real-world recordings
complements these findings by indicating a clear trend towards our
proposed self-steering pipeline as preferred choice over comparable
methods.

|                                                               |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Jakob Kienegger, Alina Mannanova, Huajian Fang, Timo Gerkmann |
| University of Hamburg, Germany                                |

## 1 Introduction

The field of speech enhancement focuses on improving the quality and
intelligibility of a recorded speech signal by suppressing noise and
reverberation artifacts. Additional interfering speakers present a
particularly challenging type of noise due to their similar and
non-stationary statistical characteristics. In such a multi-speaker
environment, the task of [tse](#id35) ([tse](#id35)) lies in identifying
and enhancing the speech signal of a specific target speaker based on
supplementary information, also known as cues. Although a range of cue
modalities have been suggested for this purpose
\[zmolikova23tse_overview\], spatial information becomes especially
popular when recordings from a microphone array are available. Commonly
under the assumption that contributing speakers are distinguishable by
their azimuth orientation to the array, a [ssf](#id31) ([ssf](#id31))
can be employed and steered in the target’s direction to extract the
desired speech signal. Compared to direct separation approaches
disentangling all speech sources at once, [ssf](#id31) have been shown
to be superior in the enhancement task \[tesch24ssf_journal\].
Especially in scenarios with stationary speakers, deep non-linear
[ssf](#id31) demonstrate exceptional performance while retaining
lightweight [nn](#id23) ([nn](#id23)) architectures
\[tesch24ssf_journal, briegleb23icospa, bohlender24sep_journal,
pandey12directional_speech_extraction, gu24rezero\].

A handful of constrained recording setups, such as a seated conference
meeting with a centered microphone array \[chen20libricss\], may
legitimate the assumption of stationary and directionally distinct
speaker locations. However, more general settings, like the dinner party
scenario considered in \[barker18chime5\], leave them unquestionably
invalid. Due to utilizing temporal context in the extraction process
\[tesch24ssf_journal, briegleb23icospa, bohlender24sep_journal,
pandey12directional_speech_extraction, gu24rezero\], the change from a
stationary to a dynamic acoustic scenario results in a significant
mismatch for data-driven [ssf](#id31). To minimize performance
degradation, speaker movement has to be included during training
\[kienegger25wg_ssf\]. The arising need for time-dependent ground truth
directional cues, which we refer to as strong guidance, bears an
additional challenge, since they are usually not available. To increase
applicability, weakly guided [tse](#id35) relies only on knowledge of
the speakers starting position by including an upstream tracking
algorithm to automate the steering of the [ssf](#id31). Although a joint
training strategy can increase robustness to cue inaccuracies, previous
work has shown that a resource-intensive tracking algorithm remains
necessary to provide sufficiently precise directional guidance and
retain strong enhancement performance \[kienegger25wg_ssf\].

While the majority of speech enhancement systems conduct offline
processing, an increasing demand in telecommunication, assistive
technologies and consumer electronics boosts the research towards
real-time capable solutions \[tan18cruse, defossez20demucs,
braun21cruse\]. Since they are often implemented as low-complexity and
causal modifications of their offline counterparts, such approaches tend
to suffer from a fundamental disadvantage due to the reduced
computational capacity \[luo19conv_tasnet, chao24SEmamba\]. However, the
sequential processing style also opens new possibilities such as
improving the enhancement performance by utilizing the extracted speech
signal from prior steps. Recent works demonstrate promising results by
introducing a temporal feedback to obtain [ar](#id34) ([ar](#id34))
[nn](#id23) architectures \[andreev23iterative_autoregression,
pan24paris_autoregressive_separation\]. Nevertheless, the inherent
non-parallelizability during training limits their applicability in
data-driven speech enhancement.

Instead of relying on computationally heavy methods utilizing
[nn](#id23) to guide the [ssf](#id31), we present a novel strategy to
improve the accuracy of a low-complexity tracking algorithm in form of a
[pf](#id41) ([pf](#id41)). Assuming a sequential processing style common
to real-time systems, we propose to utilize the enhanced speech of the
[ssf](#id31) via a temporal feedback to compensate for the limited
modeling capabilities of the [pf](#id41). To keep the training effort
light, we optimize the algorithms independently and only use a limited
number of fine-tuning steps to train the resulting [ar](#id34)
architecture in an end-to-end fashion. By evaluating our proposed
self-steering pipeline with a synthetic dataset, we can demonstrate a
drastic improvement in tracking accuracy leading to strong enhancement
performance. Complemented by a listening test with real-world
recordings, our method achieves superior speech quality and interference
suppression towards comparable approaches.

## 2 Signal Model

We model the multi-channel observation $`\mathbf{Y}`$ as mixture between
anechoic target speech signal $`\mathbf{S}`$ and noise $`\mathbf{V}`$.
The latter contains interfering speech signals, additive environmental
noise as well as the reverberant components of the target speech. In the
[stft](#id1) ([stft](#id1)) domain, this acoustic setup is resembled by

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \mathbf{Y}_{tk}=\mathbf{S}_{tk}+\mathbf{V}_{tk}\,,
       ```                                                 |     | (1) |

with $`t`$ and $`k`$ denoting frame and frequency bins respectively and
vectorization conducted over the channel dimension. In this work we set
the goal of reconstructing the anechoic target speech signal
$`\mathbf{S}_{tk}`$ at a predefined reference microphone, which we
indicate as $`S_{tk}`$. Thus, the task of [tse](#id35) lies in
recovering the speech signal $`S_{tk}`$ from the noisy observations
$`\mathbf{Y}_{tk}`$ conditioned on a speaker specific characteristic.

## 3 Spatially Guided Speaker Extraction

### 3.1 Strongly guided target speaker extraction

Spatially selective filters ([ssf](#id31)) exploit positional cues to
distinguish the target’s speech signal from interfering sources. In this
work, we abide by the common convention of restraining the cue modality
to the relative azimuth orientation $`\theta_{t}`$, referred to as
[doa](#id4) ([doa](#id4)), of the target speaker to the microphone array
\[tesch24ssf*journal, briegleb23icospa, bohlender24sep_journal\]. If
ground truth [doa](#id4) information is available, a [ssf](#id31) can be
directly employed to solve the extraction task, which we refer to as
strongly guided [tse](#id35). A common approach to recover the target
speech signal is to compute a time-frequency mask $`\mathcal{M}*{tk}`$
and extract $`S*{tk}`$ by multiplication with the corresponding
reference channel $`Y^{0}*{tk}`$ of observation $`\mathbf{Y}\_{tk}`$
\[tesch24ssf_journal, bohlender24sep_journal\],

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \widehat{S}_{tk}=\mathcal{M}_{tk}Y^{0}_{tk}\,.
       ```                                             |     | (2) |

In terms of sequential processing, the [ssf](#id31) may thus be seen as
a deterministic function $`\mathcal{F}`$ mapping current broadband input
$`\mathbf{Y}_{t}`$ and [doa](#id4) $`\theta_{t}`$ to mask values
$`\mathcal{M}_{tk}`$. Due to utilizing temporal dependencies
\[tesch24ssf*journal, briegleb23icospa, bohlender24sep_journal,
pandey12directional_speech_extraction, gu24rezero\], deep [ssf](#id31)
are parametrized by a hidden state $`\mathbf{z}*{t-1}`$ capturing
previous context in addition to the parameters $`\phi`$ of the
[nn](#id23) architecture

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{M}_{tk}=\mathcal{F}_{k}\!\left(\mathbf{Y}_{t},\theta_{t};\mathbf{z}_{t-1},\phi\right)\,.
``` |  | (3) |

Regarding the channel dimension, the [ssf](#id31) may thus be seen as a
[miso](#id45) ([miso](#id45)) system by computing a single-channel mask
$`\mathcal{M}_{tk}`$ based on multi-channel observations
$`\mathbf{Y}_{t}`$.

### 3.2 Weakly guided target speaker extraction

The dependency of strongly guided [tse](#id35) on the continuous
provision of ground truth directional information poses a great
limitation in most practical scenarios. As an alternative, weakly guided
[tse](#id35) \[kienegger25wg_ssf\] restrains the cue only to the
target’s initial orientation $`\theta_{0}`$ [wrt](#id30) the microphone
array. In order to continue using a [ssf](#id31) for the enhancement
task, an upstream tracking algorithm predicting the temporal evolution
of the [doa](#id4) $`\theta_{t}`$ becomes necessary. Due to its
well-balanced tradeoff between computational complexity and robustness,
we choose a [pf](#id41) for this task, which has already proven highly
effective in the context of acoustic speaker tracking
\[vermaak01pf_nonlinear_speaker_tracking, ward03basic_particle_filter,
dong20pf_doa_coprime\]. Modeling the tracking problem in a state-space
formulation, the [pf](#id41) recovers the [doa](#id4) $`\theta_{t}`$
encoded in state $`\mathbf{x}_{t}`$ from all available observations
$`\mathbf{Y}_{1:t}`$ and based on the initial condition
$`\mathbf{x}_{0}`$. The state $`\mathbf{x}_{t}`$ contains the
[doa](#id4) $`\theta_{t}`$ either explicitly or implicitly in a
different coordinate representation and is often complemented by
velocity or acceleration for an improved modeling of motion dynamics. A
[pf](#id41) progressively updates a discrete approximation of the
posterior $`p(\mathbf{x}_{t}|\mathbf{Y}_{1:t},\mathbf{x}_{0})`$ using
sequential importance sampling \[hagiwara21state_space_model\]

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p(\mathbf{x}_{t}|\mathbf{Y}_{1:t},\mathbf{x}_{0})\approx\sum_{n=1}^{N}w_{t}^{\scriptscriptstyle(n)}\delta\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}\!-\!\mathbf{x}_{t}^{\scriptscriptstyle(n)}\right)\,,
``` |  | (4) |

with $`\delta(\cdot)`$ denoting the Dirac delta function. The $`N`$
state samples $`\mathbf{x}_{t}^{\scriptscriptstyle(n)}`$, referred to as
particles, are drawn according to a proposal distribution
$`q\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{t}|\mathbf{Y}_{1:t},\mathbf{x}_{0:t-1}^{\scriptscriptstyle(n)}\right)`$
and the importance weights $`w_{t}^{\scriptscriptstyle(n)}`$ can be
recursively computed by imposing mild conditions on the underlying
statistical model \[arulampalam02pf_tutorial, chen04pf_sensor_fusion\].
Utilizing the approximated probability density function in
([4](#S3.E4 "Equation 4 ‣ 3.2 Weakly guided target speaker extraction ‣ 3 Spatially Guided Speaker Extraction ‣ Self-Steering Deep Non-Linear Spatially Selective Filters for Efficient Extraction of Moving Speakers under Weak Guidance"))
enables a tractable estimation of the posterior mean, which is used as
the state estimate $`\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{t}`$. The specific
[pf](#id41) formulation referred to as bootstrap filter
\[gordon93pf_bootstrap_filter\] allows for a particularly efficient
implementation by only taking the state-transition model for the
proposal distribution into account. Although the resulting state
estimates lack information from current observations, the algorithmic
simplicity makes it a popular choice for acoustic tracking tasks
\[ward03basic_particle_filter, dong20pf_doa_coprime\]. By leveraging the
state estimates of a [pf](#id41) to guide a downstream [ssf](#id31)
based on observations $`\mathbf{Y}_{t}`$ and starting direction
$`\theta_{0}`$, the [tse](#id35) pipeline emerges as concatenation of
both algorithms, see
[Fig. 1(a)](#S3.F1.sf1 "In Figure 1 ‣ 3.2 Weakly guided target speaker extraction ‣ 3 Spatially Guided Speaker Extraction ‣ Self-Steering Deep Non-Linear Spatially Selective Filters for Efficient Extraction of Moving Speakers under Weak Guidance").

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

(a) Concatenation of tracking and enhancement algorithms.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

murtagh21outdoor_walking_speed\].

## 4 Proposed method

The sequential application of tracking and enhancement algorithms may
seem like the natural approach to automate the steering of a
[ssf](#id31). While this strategy has proven successful in our previous
work on [tse](#id35) \[kienegger25wg_ssf\] as well as for the related
task of speech separation in \[bohlender24sep_journal\], it is overly
dependent on the accuracy of the upstream [doa](#id4) estimates. As a
result, computationally heavy, data-driven tracking algorithms have to
be employed to provide sufficiently precise directional information and
maintain a strong enhancement performance \[bohlender24sep_journal,
kienegger25wg_ssf\]. This additional computational overhead naturally
limits the applicability of such methods in resource-constrained
scenarios. Instead of an independent concatenation, we propose a more
dynamic interaction between tracking and enhancement algorithms. Since
the nature of sequential processing grants access to the output of the
[ssf](#id31), we introduce a temporal feedback to improve the accuracy
of a computationally lightweight [pf](#id41) as opposed to employing a
resource-intensive tracking algorithm. To retain spatial information at
the output of the [ssf](#id31), we slightly deviate from the original
formulation in
([2](#S3.E2 "Equation 2 ‣ 3.1 Strongly guided target speaker extraction ‣ 3 Spatially Guided Speaker Extraction ‣ Self-Steering Deep Non-Linear Spatially Selective Filters for Efficient Extraction of Moving Speakers under Weak Guidance")).
Rather than just for the reference channel, we propose to compute a
multi-channel mask $`\mathbfcal{M}_{tk}`$ and extract the direct path
propagated target speech signal $`\mathbf{S}_{tk}`$ by element-wise
multiplication ($`\odot`$) with the observation $`\mathbf{Y}_{tk}`$

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widehat{\mathbf{S}}_{tk}=\mathbfcal{M}_{tk}\odot\mathbf{Y}_{tk}\,.
``` |  | (5) |

Unlike the original [miso](#id45) formulation in
([2](#S3.E2 "Equation 2 ‣ 3.1 Strongly guided target speaker extraction ‣ 3 Spatially Guided Speaker Extraction ‣ Self-Steering Deep Non-Linear Spatially Selective Filters for Efficient Extraction of Moving Speakers under Weak Guidance")),
the estimates $`\widehat{\mathbf{S}}_{tk}`$ of such a [mimo](#id46)
([mimo](#id46)) strategy have already been proven to result in an
improved localization performance for stationary scenarios
\[li23gcc-speaker, chen24locselect, battula25MIMO_localization\]. Rather
than approximating the posterior based on the broadband observations
$`\mathbf{Y}_{t}`$ containing the directional information of all
speakers, the [pf](#id41) algorithm can utilize the spatial
characteristics of the target’s direct path propagation
$`p\big(\mathbf{x}_{t}|\mathbf{S}_{1:t},\mathbf{x}_{0}\big)`$. However,
due to the temporal feedback in the [ar](#id34) structure, only the
[doa](#id4) estimates from the previous frames
$`\widehat{\theta}_{t-1}`$ are accessible to the [ssf](#id31). This
necessitates a directional single-frame lookahead prediction during mask
computation, leading to the adjusted formulation

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbfcal{M}_{tk}=\mathbfcal{F}_{k}\!\left(\mathbf{Y}_{t},\theta_{t-1};\mathbf{z}_{t-1},\phi\right)\,.
``` |  | (6) |

Paired with the need to reconstruct the anechoic propagation between the
microphones of the array, the difficulty in the enhancement task
increases for the [ssf](#id31) compared to its original formulation in
([3](#S3.E3 "Equation 3 ‣ 3.1 Strongly guided target speaker extraction ‣ 3 Spatially Guided Speaker Extraction ‣ Self-Steering Deep Non-Linear Spatially Selective Filters for Efficient Extraction of Moving Speakers under Weak Guidance")).
[Figure 1(b)](#S3.F1.sf2 "In Figure 1 ‣ 3.2 Weakly guided target speaker extraction ‣ 3 Spatially Guided Speaker Extraction ‣ Self-Steering Deep Non-Linear Spatially Selective Filters for Efficient Extraction of Moving Speakers under Weak Guidance")
displays our proposed weakly guided [tse](#id35) pipeline as an
[ar](#id34) interconnection between [pf](#id41) and our [mimo](#id46)
adaption of the [ssf](#id31).

## 5 Experiments

### 5.1 Dataset

Synthetic dataset We employ a synthetic dataset consisting of noisy and
reverberant two-speaker mixtures to enable [nn](#id23) training, model
optimization and evaluation in a controlled acoustic scenario. In
particular, we use utterances from the LibriSpeech corpus
\[panayotov15librispeech\] and pair them according to the recipe in
Libri2Mix \[cosentino20librimix\]. For spatialization, we utilize
simulated [rir](#id2) in shoe-box shaped rooms based on a GPU
accelerated implementation \[diaz18gpu_rir\] of the image method
\[allen79image_method\]. We closely follow the works from Tesch et al.
\[tesch24ssf_journal, tesch22spatial_spectral_temporal_nonlinear_filter,
tesch23deep_nonliner_filter_multichannel, tesch23ssf\] by using the same
three microphone circular array of $`10\,\mathrm{cm}`$ diameter and
adhering to reverberation times between 0.2 s and 0.5 s. While retaining
the same randomized microphone placement and speaker height, we increase
the distance between array and speakers to a range of 1 m to 3 m whilst
maintaining a minimum distance of 1 m to the surrounding walls and 15 cm
among the speakers themselves. Building on our previous work
\[kienegger25wg_ssf\], we model the speaker trajectories as circular
motion with constant distance and height, allowing for a straightforward
parametrization and intuitive understanding of the spatial movement
patterns. To include directional changes and random acceleration
behavior, we choose the azimuthal motion model

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\begin{bmatrix}\theta_{t+1}\\
\dot{\theta}_{t+1}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&\hskip-5.69054pt\Delta T\\
0&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\theta_{t}\\
\dot{\theta}_{t}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}\Delta T^{2}/2\\
\Delta T\end{bmatrix}\eta_{t}\,,
``` |  | (7) |

referred to as [cv](#id32) ([cv](#id32)) or white acceleration model
\[rong03survey_target_tracking\]. The state vector $`\mathbf{x}_{t}`$ in
this linear state-space formulation consists of
$`\begin{bmatrix}\theta_{t},\dot{\theta}_{t}\end{bmatrix}^{\top}`$,
thus, azimuth orientation and instantaneous azimuth velocity,
respectively. The perturbation $`\eta_{t}`$ is a white, zero mean
Gaussian process of variance $`\sigma^{2}`$. Due to the wide range of
distances $`r`$ between speakers and microphone array, we use the
inter-frame velocity $`v_{t}`$ defined as
$`\frac{r}{\Delta T}(\theta_{t}-\theta_{t-1})`$ instead of the angular
displacement in \[kienegger25wg_ssf\] as a means to obtain a physically
meaningful parametrization for the motion model. Since the difference
$`\theta_{t}-\theta_{t-1}`$ is not affected by wrapping effects,
sequentially evaluating the linear state-space model in
([7](#S5.E7 "Equation 7 ‣ 5.1 Dataset ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Self-Steering Deep Non-Linear Spatially Selective Filters for Efficient Extraction of Moving Speakers under Weak Guidance"))
retains its Gaussianity. This makes the expected absolute velocity
$`|v_{t}|`$ at distance $`r`$ tractable and yields the closed-form
expression

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}\hskip-1.0pt\big\{|v_{t}|\big|r\big\}=\Delta T\,r\sqrt{\frac{4t-3}{2\pi}}\sigma\,.
``` |  | (8) |

We will use this correspondence to determine the standard deviation
$`\sigma`$ of the motion perturbation $`\eta_{t}`$ in
([7](#S5.E7 "Equation 7 ‣ 5.1 Dataset ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Self-Steering Deep Non-Linear Spatially Selective Filters for Efficient Extraction of Moving Speakers under Weak Guidance"))
to reach an expected absolute velocity $`|v_{t}|`$ of
1.5 $`\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}`$ at trajectory end, which
corresponds to medium walking speed
\[keller96walking_jogging_running_speed,
murtagh21outdoor_walking_speed\]. Due to the steady increase of the
expected value in
([8](#S5.E8 "Equation 8 ‣ 5.1 Dataset ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Self-Steering Deep Non-Linear Spatially Selective Filters for Efficient Extraction of Moving Speakers under Weak Guidance")),
we will only use trajectories of 5 s length and truncate the utterances
accordingly.
[Figure 2](#S3.F2 "In 3.2 Weakly guided target speaker extraction ‣ 3 Spatially Guided Speaker Extraction ‣ Self-Steering Deep Non-Linear Spatially Selective Filters for Efficient Extraction of Moving Speakers under Weak Guidance")
illustrates the resulting distribution of $`|v_{t}|`$ as well as a
selection of simulation scenarios from the test set. The step-size
$`\Delta T`$ for the temporal discretization of the trajectories is
aligned with the [stft](#id1) parametrization, for which we use a
square-root Hann window \[shimauchi14hann_window\] of length
$`32\,\mathrm{ms}`$ and $`16\,\mathrm{ms}`$ hop-size. After
spatialization, we add spherical isotropic white noise according to
\[habets07isotropic_noise_generation\] with a [snr](#id27)
([snr](#id27)) between 20 dB and 30 dB.

Recorded dataset To test generalizablity and robustness in real-world
scenarios, we also include recordings with human speakers for
evaluation. We use a microphone array matching the training
configuration in a room of
$`9.5\,\mathrm{m}\times 5.1\,\mathrm{m}\times 2.4\,\mathrm{m}`$ extent
and a reverberation time of approximately 0.35 s. Two male speakers are
instructed to simultaneously read out segments from the Rainbow Passage
\[fairbanks60rainbow_passage\] while moving in a circular trajectory.
The speakers start from opposite ends at roughly 1 m and 2 m distance
from the array, traverse to the other end of the room, and back during
the duration of their prompt. We conduct 3 recordings in total, ranging
from 10 s to 20 s. Thus, each scenario contains two speaker crossings
with velocities depending on distance to the array and length of the
prompt. To visualize the setup, we provide a video of two of the
recordings as supplementary material: https://youtu.be/aSKOSh5JZ3o

### 5.2 Algorithm implementation and optimization details

Spatially selective filter For sequential processing, recurrent
[nn](#id23) are particularly convenient as they store the temporal
context in a compact hidden state. Due to its purely recurrent nature
combined with a conceptually simple and lightweight architecture, we
choose FT-[jnf](#id22) \[tesch24ssf_journal\] as [ssf](#id31), which has
seen great popularity in a variety of applications
\[wechsler24directional_filtering_directivity_control,
briegleb24constrained_vs_unconstained_filtering,
lentz24ftjnf_head_rotation\]. Following our previous work
\[kienegger25wg_ssf\], we slightly deviate from the implementation in
\[tesch24ssf_journal\] and modify the last B-LSTM layer to obtain a
causal [ssf](#id31) while retaining roughly the intended model size. The
modifications to compute a multi-channel mask according to our
[mimo](#id46) formulation in
([6](#S4.E6 "Equation 6 ‣ 4 Proposed method ‣ Self-Steering Deep Non-Linear Spatially Selective Filters for Efficient Extraction of Moving Speakers under Weak Guidance"))
only account for a negligible increase of less than 0.1 % in model
parameters and 0.05 % in GMACs. We train FT-[jnf](#id22) in both
[miso](#id45) and [mimo](#id46) configurations for 300 epochs while
adhering to the original scheduler with an initial learning rate of
$`10^{-3}`$ and a joint time and frequency domain loss function
\[tesch24ssf_journal\]. The latter is averaged over all channels in the
[mimo](#id46) formulation. Based on our previous findings of improved
robustness to tracking inaccuracies \[kienegger25wg_ssf\], we fine-tune
the [ssf](#id31) for weakly guided [tse](#id35) in both concatenative
and self-steering pipelines for 25 additional epochs with a reduced
learning rate of $`10^{-4}`$. Instead of using iterative approaches to
avoid the non-parallelizable training of our [ar](#id34) architecture
\[andreev23iterative_autoregression,
pan24paris_autoregressive_separation\], we found that the small amount
of fine-tuning steps yielded the best performance while remaining
computationally feasible. Furthermore, we observed consistently improved
convergence when including [mae](#id13) ([mae](#id13)) as an auxiliary
loss function \[li23gcc-speaker\].

Particle filter We choose the generic bootstrap filter algorithm in
\[lehmann06pf_resampling_Neff\] as low-complexity tracking framework,
which introduces an additional conditional resampling step to counter
weight degeneracy problems \[doucet01pf_practice\]. Although providing a
zero gradient for frames affected by this resampling step, we found it
yielding better results during fine-tuning of the [ssf](#id31) than a
differentiable resampling algorithm
\[karkus18pf_differentiable_resampling\]. We use the output power of a
[das](#id42) beamformer to construct the likelihood
\[ward03basic_particle_filter\] and employ two different
state-transition densities to investigate the effect of mismatch in
motion dynamics. Thus, we include a simpler, angular [rw](#id33)
([rw](#id33)) model \[traa13wrapped_kalman_filter\] in addition to the
[cv](#id32) formulation in
([7](#S5.E7 "Equation 7 ‣ 5.1 Dataset ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Self-Steering Deep Non-Linear Spatially Selective Filters for Efficient Extraction of Moving Speakers under Weak Guidance"))
used in our synthetic dataset. We fix the number of particles $`N`$ to
50 and optimize the remaining model parameters with an exhaustive search
on the validation subset.

Fig. 3: Dependency of enhancement performance ([sisdr](#id15)) on
tracking accuracy ([mae](#id13)). Solid lines display a log-linear
regression model.

To perform a thorough assessment, we use our synthetic dataset for an
objective analysis and our recorded dataset for a subjective evaluation
conducted by human audio experts in a listening experiment. In both
cases, the [tse](#id35) methods are assessed regarding the perceptual
speech quality of the enhanced signal and the [sdr](#id14).

Synthetic dataset The availability of ground truth directional
information allows the evaluation of the different [ssf](#id31)
formulations in a strongly guided fashion, eliminating the bias from
upstream tracking inaccuracies.
[Table 1](#S6.T1 "In 6 Results ‣ Self-Steering Deep Non-Linear Spatially Selective Filters for Efficient Extraction of Moving Speakers under Weak Guidance")
compares the original [miso](#id45) (1) and our [mimo](#id46) adaption
(2) of FT-[jnf](#id22) using the intrusive metrics [pesq](#id16)
([pesq](#id16)) \[rix01pesq\] and [sisdr](#id15) ([sisdr](#id15))
\[roux19sisdr_half_baked\]. While we are on par regarding speech
quality, our proposed modifications result in a lower [sisdr](#id15)
score. This can be attributed to the additional challenge from the
delayed directional cue paired with the need of reconstructing the
anechoic inter-microphone propagation. Replacing the oracle [doa](#id4)
with estimated trajectories to evaluate the weakly guided methods, we
complement the analysis by including frame-wise [ae](#id43)
([ae](#id43)) to assess the accuracy of the [pf](#id41). In their
original formulation, both [pf](#id41) versions display great
inconsistency in their tracking performance (3, 5). Especially the
mismatched [rw](#id33) motion model (3) yields a very poor accuracy with
25 % of the [doa](#id4) estimations being more then 40° off. By
introducing our proposed [ar](#id34) interconnection, we can drastically
improve the performance of both [pf](#id41) versions (4, 6), as also
demonstrated in the example trajectories in
[Fig. 2](#S3.F2 "In 3.2 Weakly guided target speaker extraction ‣ 3 Spatially Guided Speaker Extraction ‣ Self-Steering Deep Non-Linear Spatially Selective Filters for Efficient Extraction of Moving Speakers under Weak Guidance").
[Table 1](#S6.T1 "In 6 Results ‣ Self-Steering Deep Non-Linear Spatially Selective Filters for Efficient Extraction of Moving Speakers under Weak Guidance")
and
[Fig. 4(a)](#S6.F4.sf1 "In 6 Results ‣ Self-Steering Deep Non-Linear Spatially Selective Filters for Efficient Extraction of Moving Speakers under Weak Guidance")
show how our method is able to translate the refined tracking into a
superior speech enhancement performance compared with the concatenative
approach for both perceptual quality and [sdr](#id14) criteria (4, 6).
To investigate the dependency of the two [tse](#id35) methods on the
precision of the directional cues,
[Fig. 3](#S6.F3 "In 6 Results ‣ Self-Steering Deep Non-Linear Spatially Selective Filters for Efficient Extraction of Moving Speakers under Weak Guidance")
shows the relative [sisdr](#id15) improvement in relation to
utterance-wise [mae](#id13). By indicating a stronger tie between
tracking and enhancement metrics, it becomes apparent that our
self-steering framework relies more heavily on spatial information
during the extraction process as opposed to the concatenative method.
During fine-tuning, the latter gains robustness against the imprecise
spatial conditioning and learns to leverage temporal-spectral rather
than spatial information \[kienegger25wg_ssf\].

Recorded dataset Motivated by the unavailability of clean speech signals
in the recorded dataset, a listening test with human participants rating
the enhancement performance is conducted. We design the evaluation
similar to the preference test in \[tesch24ssf_journal\] by asking
questions of the form “Example 1 is preferable over example 2” regarding
speech quality and [sdr](#id14). A total of 10 audio experts judge the
enhancement performance regarding all 6 speech signals in the 3
recordings for both [pf](#id41) versions, totaling to 12 test cases. The
results of the listening experiment in indicate a clear tendency towards
our proposed [ar](#id34) approach for both versions of the [pf](#id41).
A closer investigation unveils that the most significant performance
gain occurs for the speaker with greater distance to the array,
underlining the benefit of utilizing spatial information in low
[snr](#id27) scenarios.
